claims.claim_vi: Cache-aside: the application reads the cache, on a miss reads the data store, adds the item to the cache and returns it; on update it writes the data store and invalidates the cache entry. Many caching systems provide read-through and write-through or write-behind; cache-aside emulates read-through when they do not.
claims.verified_by: Read from a local clone of MicrosoftDocs/architecture-center at commit 8e2c239344ee753a88856800b4210a3e27ac1036, the head of its default branch when read on 2026-10-18 (a later change to that branch does not alter this URL).

claims.claim_vi: Cache-aside does not guarantee consistency: an external process can change the data store at any time; between a write and the next read a reader can briefly see stale data; write-through updates both in one operation so readers see the new value.
claims.verified_by: Read from a local clone of MicrosoftDocs/architecture-center at commit 8e2c239344ee753a88856800b4210a3e27ac1036, the head of its default branch when read on 2026-10-18 (a later change to that branch does not alter this URL).

claims.claim_vi: Two write approaches: invalidate on write, or write-through returning only after both updates succeed; treat the cache as a transient store that could disappear and do not keep valuable data only there.
claims.section: Keep the cache consistent on writes; Considerations for using caching

claims.claim_vi: With SQLite and Redis 7.0.15 (60 s TTL): a DB update without invalidation returned the old price from the cache with 60 s left; after DEL the next read got the new price; a deliberately ordered race left the DB at 150 and the cache at 120 for 60 s; write-through left both at 170; write-back lost the 210 write when Redis was shut down before the copy, leaving the DB at 200.
claims.verified_by: Experiment run by the author on 2026-10-18 on one virtual machine: Python 3.13.16 with sqlite3 in memory and a raw RESP client to Redis 7.0.15 started without persistence; the write-back flusher is the author's own loop, not a Redis feature.

claims.claim_vi: Read strategies cache-aside and read-through; write strategies write-around, write-back and write-through; often combined, such as write-around with cache-aside.
claims.verified_by: Source body read at the pinned commit.

design_notes_vi: Ba khung ghi chú: hai cách đọc, ba cách ghi, và ba kết quả thử nghiệm cho thấy mỗi cách lệch thế nào. Không vẽ mũi tên vì năm cách là lựa chọn, không phải các bước nối tiếp.
source_deviations: Source only lists the five strategies; the lesson adds definitions from Microsoft's architecture guidance and an experiment showing stale reads, a race and write-back data loss.

TTL is described as bounding the age of each cached entry, not the total stale interval: a delayed fill can store an old value after an invalidation or expiry and start a new TTL (the race of step 4); preventing it needs fills coordinated with writes, such as a version check before storing; allowing only one fill at a time is not enough, since step 4 has a single fill (author's reasoning).

Write-through freshness is scoped to writes where both updates succeed: the database and the cache are separate systems, so a failed cache write after a successful database write leaves a stale entry unless the key is invalidated (author's reasoning, consistent with Microsoft's note that write-through returns only after both updates succeed).
